title: Lean Business Analysis: Start with the Need Behind the Request
summary: Before anyone writes a requirement, find the need behind the request. A practical look at Lean BA: value, needs assessment, five whys and a business case people use.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The meeting opens with "We need a dashboard." Everyone in the room means well. Support wants fewer escalations, sales wants to see where each customer stands, and the head of the unit wants one number to look at every morning. It sounds specific enough to become a ticket by lunchtime.

Now ask one more question before anyone lists fields: which decision is this dashboard supposed to improve? The answers start to split. Maybe the real problem is slow first response. Maybe nobody owns escalated accounts. Maybe the same data gets typed into three tools. Or maybe it's a process problem that no chart will fix. That one question is most of what Lean business analysis is about, and this post walks through the rest of it.

Sources for this series: the structure follows PMI's Business Analysis for Practitioners: A Practice Guide (2015), mostly Section 2, "Needs Assessment". Section numbers below point to that book. Definitions come from the BABOK Guide glossary and the Lean Enterprise Institute lexicon.

Business analysis is something you do

The IIBA defines a business analyst as "any person who performs business analysis, no matter their job title or organizational role" (BABOK Guide glossary). On a real team that could be the PO, a PM, a designer, QA, the tech lead or the developer who asks "wait, why do they need this?" before writing a line.

That changes how you spot the gap. A team isn't missing BA because nobody has the title on the org chart. It's missing BA when people start building before they agree on what the value is, who's affected, what the constraints are, which options exist and how they'll know it worked.

The fastest check is to look at how the work arrived. Most requests show up already shaped as a solution. Each one has a question that pulls the need back out:

How the request arrivesQuestion to askWhat to write down instead
"Build this report."Which decision will this report change, and who makes it?The decision, the person who makes it and one success measure
"Automate this process."Where do people wait, redo work or work around the tool today?A sketch of the current process with the pain points marked
"The competitor has this feature."Which need of our customers would it serve?A problem statement and at least two options
"We promised it for Q3."What gets worse if we don't ship it?A short business case with the cost of waiting

Value first, then just enough analysis

Lean thinking keeps asking one thing: is this worth the team's next hour? Value isn't only revenue. It can be lower running cost, a shorter cycle time, fewer errors, less compliance risk, customers who stay, or staff who stop fighting a tool every day.

The Lean lens points back at the analysis itself. Documents nobody reads, the same approval twice, detail written months before anyone needs it, long chains of handoffs: all of that is waste too. Cutting it doesn't mean skipping the thinking. You do the smallest piece of analysis that lets the team take the next step with confidence, then you do the next piece.

Say finance asks for an approval workflow for vendor payments. The heavy version documents every field, builds a form and routes each invoice through five approval levels. The Lean version looks at the flow first. How many invoices are late, and by how much? Where do the mistakes come from? Who is waiting on whom? Which approvals does the law or the auditor require, and which ones exist only because nobody trusts the data coming in?

Sometimes the answer really is a workflow. Just as often it's cleaner vendor master data, an auto-approve rule under a threshold, a policy change, or a small queue for the exceptions.

Needs assessment: check the problem before the solution

The most expensive requirement isn't the one that takes longest to build. It's the one the team builds perfectly for the wrong need.

The PMI guide puts a whole section on this before any requirement gets written. Section 2.3 starts with the problem or opportunity: identify stakeholders, investigate, gather data, draft a situation statement, and then (2.3.5) get stakeholders to approve that statement. The last step is the one teams skip. If sales and support can't agree on a two-sentence description of the problem, they won't agree on the solution either, and it's far cheaper to find that out now.

Section 2.4 then looks at the current state: goals, root causes, the capabilities the situation needs and the gaps between those and what the organization can do today. None of this has to be heavy. For a small change it can be one page and two conversations.

Go and see the work

Lean has a word for the place where the work actually happens: gemba, Japanese for "actual place" (LEI lexicon). Go there before you write the spec.

Say you keep hearing "the CRM is slow." Sit next to a sales rep while they update a deal after a customer call. The page loads fine. What eats the time is everything around it: copying details out of an email, hunting for the right account, pinging operations for the contract status, guessing which field feeds the pipeline report. "Slow" was true. It wasn't precise enough to build anything from.

Five whys, used lightly

The Lean Enterprise Institute describes 5 Whys as asking why repeatedly "to get beyond the obvious symptoms to discover the root cause" (LEI lexicon). The PMI guide lists it in 2.4.4.1, next to cause-and-effect diagrams. You don't need a workshop for it. Five honest answers in a doc are enough:

  1. Why are renewals late? Account managers don't see contract risk early enough.
  2. Why not? The warning signs live in support tickets and billing notes.
  3. Why doesn't the CRM show them? The integration only syncs customer identity and invoice status.
  4. Why was risk left out? The original CRM project was built for sales forecasting.
  5. Why did nobody raise renewals? Customer success wasn't treated as a main stakeholder back then.

It may still end up as a dashboard. But now it has a sharp job: show renewal risk from support, billing and usage data before each account review. One caution: five whys follows one chain of causes, and real problems often have several. If two people get different chains, draw a cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram and look at them side by side.

A business case is a decision tool

The BABOK glossary defines a business case as "a justification for a course of action based on the benefits to be realized by using the proposed solution, as compared to the cost, effort, and other considerations to acquire and live with that solution" (BABOK Guide glossary). "Live with" is the part teams forget. A custom tool costs its build and then every year of upkeep after it.

It doesn't need to be thick. A few pages that let someone say yes, no or not yet are plenty. PMI's Section 2.5 gives a sensible order:

  • Offer alternative options, and include doing nothing (2.5.2).
  • Write down the constraints, assumptions and risks for each option (2.5.3).
  • Check feasibility: operational, technical, cost and time (2.5.4).
  • Recommend one option, using a weighted ranking if the choice is close (2.5.5).
  • Then run the cost-benefit numbers for that option: payback period, ROI, IRR, NPV (2.5.6).

A weighted ranking is a plain table with honest columns. Here's a rough one for the vendor payment case:

OptionValueSpeedRiskMaintainabilityComment
Build a custom workflowHighMediumMediumMediumFits the process exactly, and someone owns it for years
Configure the tool we already haveMediumHighLowHighA good first step if the process can bend a little
Buy a specialist productHighMediumMediumHighWorth it if this capability matters long term
Do nothingLowHighHighHighStill a choice, so name the risk you're accepting

Notice the order in PMI's list: numbers come last, for the option you already picked on fit and feasibility. ROI and NPV add discipline, but they serve judgment and can't replace it. A spreadsheet with four decimal places built on weak assumptions is riskier than a rough estimate that says plainly what it doesn't know yet.

A short checklist before anyone writes a requirement

  • Can you state the problem without naming a solution?
  • Have you watched the work happen, or only heard the complaint?
  • Do the main stakeholders agree with that problem statement?
  • Do you know who benefits, who has to change how they work and who might lose something?
  • Are there at least two options on the table, including doing nothing?
  • What's the smallest piece of evidence that would tell you to keep going?

Try it on the next request that lands in your queue: before anyone opens the ticket template, write the problem in two sentences with no solution in them and send it to the requester. If they reply "yes, exactly," you're ready for requirements. The next post in this series covers that part: planning the analysis, mapping stakeholders and getting past the stated request.

faqs.a: It's business analysis done with a Lean mindset: start from the value a change should create, cut waste in the analysis itself (unread documents, duplicate approvals, detail written too early) and do just enough analysis to make the next decision with confidence.

faqs.q: How is needs assessment different from requirements gathering?
faqs.a: Needs assessment checks that you have the right problem before anyone designs a solution. In PMI's Business Analysis for Practitioners it covers stakeholders, a situation statement the stakeholders approve, root cause analysis, capability gaps and a recommended option. Requirements gathering usually starts after a solution direction has been picked.

faqs.q: What should a lightweight business case include?
faqs.a: The problem, who it affects, at least two options including doing nothing, the constraints, assumptions and risks of each, a feasibility check, the recommended option and how you'll measure success. Add cost-benefit numbers such as payback period or ROI for the recommended option, and include what it costs to live with the solution after launch.

faqs.q: Does Lean BA mean less documentation?
faqs.a: It means documentation with a job. Keep what helps people understand the problem, agree on it or make a decision, and drop what nobody reads. A two-sentence problem statement that the stakeholders approved is often worth more than a long spec.

faqs.q: Who does business analysis if the team has no BA?
faqs.a: Whoever is doing the work of understanding the need. The BABOK glossary defines a business analyst as any person who performs business analysis, no matter their job title, so on many teams it's the product owner, a designer, QA or the tech lead.
